Article Title: Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang can't stop making fun of Google, says who is ...
Article Text:
Meta AI head

The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at Google

Where the gains came from

The cost advantage

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.Wang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).According to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.Beyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee, recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini. Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: From DJ Blasts To Drilling Noise, Nine complaints on ‘Noise-Free Nagpur’ in 2 days
Article Text:
Noise pollution





Nagpur: From blaring DJs and loudspeakers to construction drilling and the screech of an iron-rod cutting machine, citizens have flagged various incidents on the “Noise Free Nagpur” portal within just two days of its launch. At least nine complaints have been received since the online platform went live on Wednesday, with grievances registered across five police stations.The complaints underline that noise concerns extend beyond the usual festive-season complaints against DJs and loudspeakers. Three complaints filed from Kotwali police station limits on Sept 4 included two specifically mentioning loud DJ music and announcements. Another complaint from Ajni police station limits concerned a loudspeaker.A complaint filed at Sitabuldi police station on Sept 5 concerned noise from a construction site in a residential area, while another complaint registered at Bajaj Nagar police station was against loud construction and drilling noise.At Sadar police station, a citizen complained about the operation of an iron-rod cutting machine, highlighting how commercial and construction activity can also become a source of disturbance for residents.The portal dashboard showed all nine complaints as “escalated”, indicating that they had moved beyond the initial response level under the platform’s time-bound grievance mechanism.One of the complaints indicated at the intensity of noise being reported. The complaint at Kotwali police station against DJ music recorded a peak sound level of 92.4 decibels and an average of 84.2 decibels during a 41-second recording. The portal flagged the reading as a severe noise level and indicated that the CPCB permissible limit had been breached.The complaint was submitted on Sept 4 at around 9.41pm and was initially assigned to the police station. After the stipulated 30-minute service level agreement (SLA) was breached, it was escalated to the ACP and subsequently to the DCP.The “Noise Free Nagpur” system (https://noisefreenagpur.in) was jointly developed and implemented by Nagpur Municipal Corporation (NMC) and Nagpur police following directions of the Nagpur bench of Bombay High Court. The platform was developed by NMC IT officer Swapnil Lokhande.NMC recently reduced the response time from three hours to 30 minutes at each level. Complaints are automatically routed to the jurisdictional police inspector.Citizens can lodge complaints against DJs, loudspeakers, public events, construction and drilling, machinery, generators, firecrackers, unnecessary honking and modified silencers. They can upload photographs, videos or audio recordings and use the live decibel meter to capture the sound level.The portal records the complaint’s timestamp, GPS location and escalation history, allowing citizens and authorities to track its progress through a reference number.The early complaints come ahead of Ganeshotsav and the festive season, when the use of DJs, loudspeakers and other amplified sound generally increases.
Article Summary: At least nine complaints have been received since the online platform went live on Wednesday. Three complaints filed from Kotwali police station limits on Sept 4 included two specifically mentioning loud DJ music and announcements. A complaint filed at Sitabuldi police station on Sept 5 concerned noise from a construction site in a residential area.

Article Title: Four private Michigan islands spanning 520 acres hit the market for $2.3 million; the deal includes a home, two boats and land protected by a conservation easement
Article Text:
Turnkey residence with panoramic water views

Environmental protection and native wildlife corridors

Remote border real estate market dynamics

A private group of four islands covering 520 acres along the US-Canada border has been listed for $2.3 million. The sale includes a renovated home, machinery, two boats and a mainland dock slip. Located in Potagannissing Bay and the St Marys River near Drummond Island, the property includes Burnt Island, Wilson Island, Claw Island and Harris Island, according to the New York Post and listing brokers Coldwell Banker Schmidt Realtors and @properties. Burnt Island makes up most of the property and contains the main home and other facilities. Wilson, Claw and Harris Islands form a smaller group nearby. The large estate combines private wilderness with permanent conservation protections and offers about 2,000 feet of waterfront along northern Michigan’s international water boundary.The main home sits on the southern tip of Burnt Island and offers 270-degree views of the surrounding waterways and shipping lanes. Originally built as an island retreat, the 2,131-square-foot house was fully renovated inside and outside between 2017 and 2018. The home has three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. It is being sold turnkey, with furnishings and working equipment included in the sale. "If you have ever dreamed of owning your own island, here's your chance to own four!" the listing from Gaslight Group Properties and Coldwell Banker says."Set along the picturesque northern border in the St Mary's River & Potagannissing Bay, this group of islands is truly special." The sale also includes a utility truck, a Kubota tractor with a brush hog attachment, a riding lawn mower, a separate sauna building and two motorboats to help with maintenance and travel between the islands. The property’s two main docks and protective breakwalls were rebuilt between 2022 and 2023. The sale also comes with a dedicated boat slip at DeTour Village on the Michigan mainland, providing regular access to the islands.One of the main features of the 520-acre property is the balance between private use and long-term environmental protection. About 420 acres across the four islands are covered by a permanent conservation easement held by the Little Traverse Conservancy, a regional land trust in northern Michigan. The easement prevents future commercial subdivision and major construction, helping protect native forests and wildlife habitats. The owner still has about 100 acres of unrestricted land around the home, outbuildings and shorelines for private recreation and personal use. "Most of the 520 acres is protected by a conservation easement with Little Traverse Conservancy but about 100 of the acres and the shorelines are yours to explore," according to the official Northern Michigan MLS listing. The islands feature private walking trails, wild fruit orchards with apple and crabapple trees, milkweed meadows and quiet coves. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters, beavers, coyotes and white-tailed deer. The waters around Potagannissing Bay are also an established fishing area, supporting native populations of walleye, smallmouth bass, yellow perch and cisco.The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. People staying on Burnt Island can often watch commercial Great Lakes freighters travelling through the nearby St Marys River channel, which connects Lake Superior with Lake Huron. Real estate agents who specialise in northern Michigan waterfront properties say turnkey island estates with mainland facilities, such as dedicated marina slips, can command higher prices because of the challenges of maintaining remote properties. Listing agents Sam DeCamp and Anna DeCamp of Gaslight Group Properties are continuing to show the property to potential buyers looking for private conservation retreats.
Article Summary: The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters and coyotes.

Article Title: Scientists discover nearly 1 billion tons of water locked inside Utah's rocky glaciers, using gravity measurements to map ice buried beneath mountain debris
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

A glacier hidden beneath rocks

Scientists used gravity to see underground ice

Images of Timpanogos Rock Glacier. (a) Photo of Timpanogos Rock Glacier on 1 August 1925, showing the rock glacier (right side of the frame) flanked by seasonal snow (University of Utah Photo Archives)(b) Image of a moulin-like feature on the upper portion of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, with layers of firn separated by thin debris layers. We expect that the firn transitions to ice at depth. (Image: University of Utah Photo Archives)

One Utah rock glacier holds hundreds of swimming pools of water

A hidden water reserve facing a changing climate

At first glance, Utah's rocky mountain slopes may look completely dry, with loose stones and boulders covering the ground. But beneath some of those rocks lies an enormous store of frozen water. Researchers have now estimated that Utah's rock glaciers contain about 0.99 gigatonnes, or nearly 1 billion tons, of water equivalent. These unusual formations are bodies of ice buried beneath thick layers of rock and debris, allowing them to survive in places where conventional glaciers cannot. The discovery comes from a study of the Timpanogos Rock Glacier beneath Mount Timpanogos, where scientists used subtle changes in Earth's gravitational field to reconstruct what was hidden underground. Published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, the research was led by Bronson Cvijanovich with Michael S. Thorne, Surya Pachhai, Leif S. Anderson, Ivan Tochimani-Hernandez, Christian L. Hardwick and Tonie van Dam, from the University of Utah and Utah Geological Survey.Rock glaciers look nothing like the bright, exposed ice fields people normally associate with glaciers. They are instead masses of ice covered by layers of loose rocks and debris, with the ice slowly moving downhill beneath the surface.That rocky blanket can insulate the ice from warmth and sunlight, allowing these formations to persist in mountain environments that may no longer support conventional glaciers. The researchers explain in their study, ‘ The Internal Ice Content of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, Utah, USA From 3-D Bayesian Inversion of Gravity Data, ’ that rock glaciers are increasingly important as climate change reduces conventional glacier ice. They can store water, provide refuges for cold-adapted species and, if destabilised, create hazards for communities below. Yet scientists have struggled to determine exactly how much ice these formations contain because their rocky surfaces hide their interiors.To look beneath Timpanogos Rock Glacier, the team turned to a method that does not require drilling through the entire formation. They collected 232 gravity measurements across the site and used a three-dimensional Bayesian inversion to reconstruct the hidden structure. Ice is substantially less dense than the surrounding bedrock, so a sufficiently large buried ice mass creates a tiny but measurable reduction in gravitational acceleration. By mapping these variations, researchers could estimate where the ice-rich material was located and how thick it was. The study also found an estimated ice volume of about 1.55 million cubic metres, with an average thickness of 18.8 metres. The researchers' preferred model indicates that the entire rock glacier is about 72% ice by volume, while its ice core is approximately 83% ice.The amount of ice beneath Mount Timpanogos is difficult to visualise, so the researchers compared it with something more familiar. Their estimated 1.55 million cubic metres of ice is roughly equivalent to the volume of 600 Olympic-sized swimming pools. More importantly, Timpanogos Rock Glacier provided the researchers with a way to estimate the hidden water stored across many similar formations. Using their measurements alongside data from other rock glaciers, the team developed a new area-volume relationship. In the research this method produced an estimate of 0.99 gigatonnes of water equivalent for Utah's intact rock glaciers. The western United States was estimated to contain about 11.92 gigatonnes, while intact rock glaciers worldwide could hold approximately 48.03 gigatonnes.The discovery matters because rock glaciers could become increasingly important as conventional glaciers retreat. Their insulating debris can protect buried ice for longer, making them relatively resilient stores of frozen water in warming mountain environments. But the researchers also caution that their estimates are not perfectly complete. Persistent snow and steep terrain prevented gravity measurements in the upper reaches of Timpanogos Rock Glacier, meaning the calculated ice volume is likely a lower estimate of the total. The study also notes uncertainties in modelling the relationship between ice thickness and density. Even so, the findings reveal a substantial reservoir that is almost invisible from the surface. As temperatures rise and mountain ice changes, understanding these buried stores could become increasingly important for water resources, ecosystems and assessing hazards in alpine regions.
Article Summary: Scientists used gravity to see underground ice beneath Utah's Timpanogos Rock Glacier. They estimated that Utah's rock glaciers contain about 0.99 gigatonnes, or nearly 1 billion tons, of water equivalent. Discovery matters because rock glaciers could become increasingly important as climate change reduces conventional glacier ice.

Article Title: Millions of hours of Ukraine drone data being used to train AI: Report
Article Text:
Ukraine's battlefield data fuels new AI market (AI-generated image)

Why battlefield data is so valuable

From war machines to civilian technology

The problem: Who owns battlefield experience?

A new AI market without clear rules

Ukraine’s war with Russia is generating a resource that could outlive the conflict itself. Reports suggest that vast amounts of battlefield data are increasingly being used to train artificial intelligence systems, creating a new and largely unregulated market around the technology.Every drone flight can generate thousands of data points, including images, video, sensor readings and information about how operators respond to changing conditions. Ukraine has begun turning those records into training material for AI systems, giving defence companies access to real-world combat experience.According to an analysis by MIT Technology Review, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence announced in January that it would make millions of data points collected during tens of thousands of drone flights available to military contractors and commercial companies. Since then, more than 100 companies and the UK government have gained access to the data.The UK’s access came through a new defence partnership with Ukraine that allows British universities and companies to work with battlefield data through Ukraine’s AI Avengers Labs. The platform contains millions of frames collected from cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield.AI systems need enormous amounts of data to learn how to operate when conditions are unpredictable.The most useful training material often comes from situations that are difficult to recreate in controlled environments, when visibility suddenly disappears, communications are jammed or an operator has to improvise.War produces those situations constantly.MIT Technology Review noted that battlefield data therefore offers defence companies a volume of machine experience that laboratories cannot easily replicate. Ukraine’s constantly changing terrain and combat conditions create source of material for developing more robust autonomous systems.That has also opened the door to commercial applications. US-based Enabled Intelligence has already made more than half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available for AI training, with potential applications spanning military and commercial systems.The process effectively turns combat experience into a reusable training asset: operational records are processed, labelled and matched with information about what a drone or its operator was doing, creating datasets that can then be fed into new AI models.The development is part of a broader shift in which technologies originally developed for civilian use are being adapted for warfare, while the data generated on the battlefield can eventually flow back into civilian industries.Drones operating in Ukraine, for instance, have generated data from signal-jammed and otherwise difficult environments. Some technologies trained using such conditions are already being applied in agriculture, including systems used to map and survey fields in areas where conventional connectivity is limited.This creates what MIT Technology Review described as a new loop: commercial technology enters warfare, generates data under extreme conditions, and that data can then return to the commercial sector as an input for the next generation of products.The precedent is not entirely new. US drones operating over Syria and Yemen generated data that helped inform early generations of semiautonomous military systems.Military laws regulate how countries conduct war, but they say far less about what happens after information generated during combat is extracted, packaged and licensed to private companies.Ukraine has introduced controls around access to its battlefield datasets, but there is no broader regulatory framework governing what happens after that information is absorbed into AI models and potentially moves into civilian markets.The data can contain images, locations and sensor records involving soldiers, civilians and people caught in attacks. Those individuals never necessarily agreed to have their experiences turned into training material for products that could be developed and sold years later.There is also a deeper economic concern. Frontline countries bear the physical cost of generating this data, while companies and wealthier countries far from the fighting could ultimately capture much of its commercial value. That could create an extractive market in which the human risks of war become a source of digital capital.Unlike conventional datasets, where the movement of information can sometimes be tracked, it can become nearly impossible to determine where specific battlefield information went after being incorporated into an AI system.MIT Technology Review argues that battlefield data should therefore not be treated like ordinary commercial material. Governments granting access could instead treat it more like a controlled weapons transfer, tracking its origin, licensing users and restricting onward sharing.
Article Summary: Ukraine’s war with Russia is generating a resource that could outlive the conflict itself. Every drone flight can generate thousands of data points, including images, video, sensor readings and information about how operators respond to changing conditions. Ukraine has begun turning those records into training material for AI systems.

What did researchers find around the wreck

How does the wreck affect the seabed around it

Significance of the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ for future marine research

More than eight decades after the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ sank in Albania’s Vlora Bay, its rusting remains have become part of a busy underwater ecosystem. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities, with fish, sponges, sea squirts and other marine life using its hard surfaces. The sighting was the first confirmed record in Vlora Bay since 1996. According to the research article published in Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability titled ‘ First assessments on marine geomorphology and bio-colonization through the study and survey of the wreck of the Hospital Ship “Po” along the Albanian coasts (Vlora Bay) ’ recorded the non-indigenous devil firefish and evidence of squid spawning around the wreck. Most strikingly, a critically endangered Mediterranean monk seal was photographed resting inside sheltered cavities of the ship in August 2023. Lying at depths of 33 to 37 metres within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine Protected Area, the wreck is now being studied not only as a remnant of wartime history but also as a structure that shapes local marine habitats and seabed conditions.The Hospital Ship ‘Po’ now supports a dense marine community in Vlora Bay, with more than 80% of its hard surface covered by biological growth. Researchers identified 54 taxa living on the wreck’s structure. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel. Fish surveys recorded 28 species from 14 families, including dusky groupers, morays, seabass, wrasses, seabreams and barracuda.Juvenile common two-banded seabream, painted comber and striped red mullet were also observed around the structure. The bow supported more complex assemblages than midship and stern areas.Among the most notable observations was the presence of the devil firefish, Pterois miles, a non-indigenous species recorded on the wreck’s hard surfaces. Researchers observed up to seven individuals at the same time. The survey also found large gelatinous egg clusters attributed to Ommastrephidae, likely Illex coindetii, attached to vertical surfaces at depths of 22 to 25 metres. These observations suggest the wreck may provide conditions suitable for reproduction and shelter. The study further recorded a transient Mediterranean monk seal, Monachus monachus, resting inside sheltered cavities in the upper structure.The wreck does more than provide a surface for marine organisms. Its position also appears to influence the seabed around it. The 134.98-metre vessel lies upright at 33 to 37 metres depth and remains almost perpendicular to the dominant northwest-southeast water currents. Surveys identified a scour hollow reaching 2.1 metres below the reference seabed on the upstream side. Behind the stern, sediment formed a depositional trail extending about 45 metres. Sediment samples showed medium sand of about 350 micrometres at reference sites, while fine silt-clay particles below 63 micrometres occurred close to the wreck.The researchers describe the findings as an early step towards understanding how historic wrecks function within marine ecosystems. They developed two preliminary measures, the Geometric-Geomorphological Wreck Effect Index and the Ecological Hotspot Value Index, to summarise observations at the site. The ecological index was 0.83, based on benthic diversity, biological coverage and selected indicator groups.
Article Summary: Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel.

Article Title: Meet Andy Barrett, the 13-year-old Ohio student who turned a school 3D printer into a small business, selling 150 fidget toys and raising money for epilepsy awareness
Article Text:
Photo: Andy BarrettPhoto credit: https://lp.constantcontactpages.com

From classroom tool to business idea

Designing and printing the toys

Selling 150 fidget toys

Why epilepsy awareness?

Profits into impact

Support from school and family

What’s next for Andy?

Most 13-year-olds walk into middle school tech lab thinking about passing their next assignment or making something cool to toss into their backpack. Andy Barrett, an eighth-grader at Granville Middle School in Ohio, saw something entirely different when he looked at his school's 3D printer. He saw an opportunity to build a business that could actually help people. Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business right from his classroom. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours. Instead of pocketing the money for video games or new shoes, he directed every cent of his profits toward epilepsy awareness and research.The project began inside a standard technology and engineering class, the kind of room where students typically learn the basics of digital design and manufacturing. In most middle schools, a 3D printer gets used to produce simple trinkets, small keychains, or prototype parts for short-term grading rubrics. Andy realised early on that the technology offered far more potential.He noticed how popular fidget toys had become among his peers. Kids were constantly looking for tactile objects to help them focus, manage stress, or simply keep their hands occupied during long school days. Rather than buying mass-produced plastic toys from big store shelves, Andy figured he could design his own versions, customise them, and offer them directly to people around him.Bringing a digital design to life takes far more work than simply hitting print. After getting approval from his teachers, Andy spent long hours in the school lab perfecting his fidget toys. He learnt the software from scratch, playing around with different shapes, hinges and textures, so the finished pieces felt comfortable to hold. The learning curve was sharp. He'd tackle clogged nozzles, peeling plastic, and failed prints tossed into the scrap bin. After printing, each piece required a bit of handwork, like trimming away excess material or smoothing out any rough spots. Andy relied on his friends to test early prototypes, modifying his designs according to their feedback until the toys were rugged and dependable.When the other kids saw the bright, custom toys in action, word spread through the hallways in a hurry. What began as a few casual sales has turned into a steady stream of orders, with teachers, school staff and neighbours getting in on the act. Andy quickly found himself running a real business, keeping track of customers and money, fitting in printing time around his classes. When he finally hit his goal of selling 150 toys, he had built a functioning, thriving business right out of his middle school science lab.What truly set Andy apart was his motivation. From the very beginning, he decided that the proceeds would go directly to funding epilepsy research and supporting organisations that help families dealing with the condition. The choice was deeply personal. Andy knows people in his life who have epilepsy, a neurological disorder that causes unpredictable, recurring seizures. Seeing friends or family struggle with the difficulties of the condition gave him a clear view that it can be hard. In addition to the physical toll of medical appointments and daily medications, people with epilepsy often face social stigma, anxiety and a general lack of understanding from those around them. Andy saw his fidget toys as a creative way to start conversations, educate his peers and create meaningful support for a cause that doesn’t get enough attention in middle school halls.Andy turned profits into donations and simple plastic gadgets into tools for social good. While the dollar figure alone was an impressive accomplishment for an eighth-grader, the educational impact went so much deeper. Every transaction became a moment to talk about epilepsy. Classmates who bought a toy were not just getting a fun accessory for their desk, they were learning about a neurological condition that affects millions of children and adults worldwide. Andy proved that you do not need a massive corporate budget to make a meaningful difference in your community.Projects like this rarely succeed in a vacuum. Andy’s initiative flourished because his surrounding community chose to champion his effort. His teachers provided the trust, classroom access, and flexibility needed to run the 3D printers during free hours. His family helped him plan the sales, manage the money responsibly and donate the proceeds to real non-profits. His friends and neighbours showed up as excited customers. This collaborative spirit shows what’s possible when schools and communities support young people to pursue true passion projects.Andy is 13 years old and still in middle school. He has many years of learning and experimentation ahead of him. He could keep selling fidget toys. He could expand into other 3D-printed products. Or he could channel his energy into new causes and new projects. Whatever he does next, he’ll take experience of running a small, purpose-led company with him. The 150 fidget toys he sold and the money he raised for epilepsy awareness are real proof right now that even one student can use a classroom tool for good, if he has the right support and motivation.
Article Summary: Andy Barrett, an eighth-grader at Granville Middle School in Ohio, saw an opportunity to build a business that could actually help people. Armed with basic design software, brightly colored plastic filament, and a personal drive to make a difference, Andy launched a micro-business. He designed, printed, and sold roughly 150 custom fidget toys to fellow students, teachers, and neighbours.

Article Title: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity; decades later scientists found the plantations were changing groundwater but not the soil nature
Article Text:
Eucalyptus cladocalyx ‘nana’. Image Credit: ERA Nurseries

How did eucalyptus plantations change groundwater and soil salinity in Australia

The groundwater changed, but the saline seep remained

Why didn't the eucalyptus trees solve the salinity problem

Image Credit: AI generated

Some eucalyptus species performed better over 15 years

nana

A long-term lesson from Australia's eucalyptus plantations

Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater processes behind the problem. A long-running experiment in south-western Australia later showed that the effects of such plantations were more complicated than simply planting trees and waiting for the land to recover. Researchers established a mixed eucalyptus plantation above a saline seep in 1976 and monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped. Published in ‘ Agricultural Water Management ,’ this comprehensive study reveals that effective land management requires understanding complex underground hydrological systems, cautioning against oversimplified solutions to persistent environmental challenges like soil salinity.The findings suggested that tree water use alone could not overcome the deeper flow of groundwater carrying dissolved salts toward the surface. Local geology, groundwater pathways and seasonal water availability all influenced whether planting trees could actually reduce salinity in the affected landscape. Ultimately, the study underscores that tackling soil salinity demands site-specific strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all reforestation approach.The study examined a plantation established on about 12% of a small farm catchment. The trees were planted above a saline seep, an area where salty groundwater had reached or approached the surface and damaged the land. The researchers wanted to identify eucalyptus species that could use large amounts of water and potentially help reclaim such affected areas. According to the study, the catchment contained two important groundwater systems. One was a deep aquifer in the lower part of the landscape and the other, a shallower seasonal aquifer. The researchers monitored changes in groundwater level and salinity using piezometers, allowing them to follow how conditions changed as the plantation developed.The results showed that the plantation was having a noticeable effect on water use. Changes in groundwater levels, along with observations of perched water, indicated that the trees were using more water than the nearby crop and pasture vegetation. This was an important finding because the basic idea behind planting trees in salt-affected agricultural landscapes was that trees could alter the movement of water through the soil. If less water moved downwards into the groundwater system, or if trees removed more water from the landscape, they could potentially help limit the processes that bring salt towards the surface.The researchers found that the plantation influenced groundwater chemistry as well as water levels. Chloride concentrations in the deep aquifer fell by approximately 20% between 1977 and 1984. The decline was greater at the middle of the slope than further downslope. This suggested that conditions beneath the catchment were changing, although the changes were not uniform across the landscape. At the same time, the study found larger stores of salt in the soil downslope than at the middle of the slope. There was also visual evidence that salt continued to be discharged extensively through the saline seep throughout the experiment. In other words, the trees were clearly affecting the local water system, but their presence did not bring the expected recovery of the seep. The research showed why this distinction matters. A plantation may increase water use and change groundwater conditions without having enough influence over the particular underground system responsible for a saline area. The findings also suggested that surface changes alone could not explain what was happening beneath the catchment, where groundwater pathways controlled the movement of salt.One of the most important findings of the study concerned the location of the plantation. The researchers identified the site's underground geology as a significant reason why the trees failed to control the seepage. The plantation was located in an area where the relevant aquifer appeared to be ‘confined.’ That meant the groundwater system beneath the site was not easy for the trees to influence in the way researchers had hoped. This finding highlighted a practical limitation of tree-based approaches to salinity. Planting species that use substantial amounts of water may not be enough on its own. The location of groundwater, the way water moves through underground layers and the position of the plantation within the wider landscape can all affect the outcome. The study therefore showed that managing salinity is not simply a question of selecting the thirstiest trees. Understanding the underground environment is equally important.The experiment also compared the performance of different eucalyptus species. The original aim was to rank species partly according to water use, which the researchers assessed through factors including leaf area and survival. Tree growth was rapid during the early years of the experiment, continuing strongly until 1981. After that, growth declined. 15 years later, four species emerged as the most promising among those tested. These included ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx var.,’ ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx,’ ‘Eucalyptus occidentalis’ and ‘Eucalyptus sargentii.’ Their performance did not mean that the plantation had solved the saline seep problem. Instead, it showed that some species were better suited than others to the demanding conditions of the site. A tree can survive well and use considerable amounts of water while still being unable to alter a groundwater system enough to stop salt from reaching the surface.The 15-year experiment provided a more realistic picture of what tree planting could not achieve in salt-affected farmland. The eucalyptus plantation used more water than the surrounding vegetation, and conditions in the deep groundwater system also shifted, including a significant fall in chloride concentration. Yet the saline seep continued to discharge salt. As per the study, this outcome was due to the underground conditions beneath the plantation. The research pointed towards a broader lesson that the success of planting trees depends not only on the trees, but also on the landscape in which they are planted. For areas struggling with rising groundwater and soil salinity, the findings suggest that planting eucalyptus can be a useful tool, but it is not a solution. Trees can change groundwater behaviour, without necessarily controlling the source of the problem. Only by monitoring the plantation for many years were researchers able to see both the benefits of greater tree water use and the limits imposed by the site's hidden groundwater system.
Article Summary: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity. Researchers monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped.

Article Title: Scotland quarry expansion uncovered a 2,000-year-old woman’s grave; archaeologists were stunned by its carefully built stone walls
Article Text:
'Beautifully made' Iron Age burial site containing the skeleton of a woman at a quarry in Sutherland. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Discovery of the 2,000-year-old unique burial in Scotland

What did the Iron Age grave of a woman look like

Further analysis is being carried out on the grave. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Absence of objects in the women’s grave

What can the skeleton reveal about the woman

A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scotland, revealing an unexpected glimpse of life and death at that time. Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The grave was found within an area where evidence of ancient settlement has also been identified, including features that may once have supported timber roundhouses. What caught the archaeologists’ attention was the unusual quality of the stonework. The structure was so neatly built that, at first, the team wondered whether it could have been modern. Instead, the construction style and archaeological evidence pointed towards the Iron Age, with the woman apparently having remained undisturbed for centuries beneath the ground.The discovery was made during archaeological work connected with the planned expansion of the Evelix quarry near Dornoch. According to the BBC, HAS was working for local quarry firm ‘GF Job’ when archaeologists encountered the stone-lined structure.The location was already considered archaeologically important. The Highland Historic Environment Record shows that the wider Evelix area has produced evidence of prehistoric activity, including burial remains, cremation burials, pottery and features linked to earlier settlement. This newly discovered structure stood out because of its carefully constructed stone lining. Instead of looking like a simple hole dug into the ground, it had been deliberately built with substantial masonry. As per the BBC, archaeologist Lynne McKeggie said the team initially thought the structure might be modern because of how well the stonework had been put together. That first impression quickly changed once the remains and other evidence were examined.The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep, according to the BBC. A small stone staircase formed part of the construction, adding another feature to the burial. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. The archaeological team believes the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age. The careful construction is one of the most striking parts of the discovery. The stonework had been fitted together so neatly that the archaeologists described the structure as ‘beautifully made.’ Its appearance raises questions about why so much effort was put into creating it.The Highland Historic Environment Record provides an important background to the discovery. The people who built the structure were working without modern machinery, yet they created a substantial stone-lined space with a staircase. The result survived beneath the landscape for roughly two millennia before quarry-related archaeological work exposed it. Earlier archaeological work at the Evelix quarry area had already shown that the landscape contained evidence of prehistoric activity.The burial does not appear to have contained a collection of obvious grave goods. The BBC reported that no objects were found inside the structure, although archaeologists did identify a large quantity of animal bone. The absence of objects does not make the discovery less significant. In fact, it leaves more questions about the purpose of the structure and the circumstances surrounding the woman's burial. The animal remains may provide useful evidence as further analysis takes place. The construction itself can offer clues about the importance of the site to the people who used it. The wider archaeological record for Evelix also shows that prehistoric burials and settlement activity had previously occurred in the area.The remains could eventually provide a much more personal picture of the woman who was buried at the site. BBC reports that GF Job is funding further analysis of the human remains. Specialists will study the skeleton in greater detail, with the aim of learning more about the individual and the circumstances surrounding the burial. For now, many details remain unknown. Her exact age, background and life story cannot be established simply from the discovery itself. Those answers will depend on the scientific examination still to come. Archaeologists are using photographs and 3D scans to preserve information about the structure and the position of the remains.Once the further analysis has been carried out, the skeleton will be made available to Treasure Trove Scotland for potential allocation to a museum. What began as archaeological work ahead of a modern quarry expansion has revealed a carefully constructed resting place that had remained hidden for around 2,000 years. The woman's identity may never be known, but the grave itself has survived as a quiet reminder of the care and effort that people in Iron Age Sutherland could invest in remembering their dead.
Article Summary: Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. Article Title: In 2018, a University of Hawaii study compared green and white roofs in Honolulu and found green roofs stayed cooler during the hottest hours

How much cooler was the green roof than the white roof

How the green roof reduced heat

The green roof cooled nearby air during the day

In 2018, a University of Hawaii study in Honolulu found that a planted green roof could stay noticeably cooler than a conventional white roof, particularly during the hottest part of the day. The research compared an existing white rooftop with a green roof covered in sedum plants, recording temperatures at the roof surface and in the air above it over 36 consecutive days. The results showed a clear difference: the green roof’s average daytime surface temperature was 4.1°F lower than that of the white roof, while its peak temperature was 18.5°F lower. The cooling effect was also detected in the air immediately above the roof, where temperatures 2 ft above the green surface averaged 3.4°F lower during the day. The findings suggest that vegetation can help limit rooftop heat and moderate nearby air temperatures, offering another possible way to tackle Honolulu’s urban heat island effect in cities and dense neighbourhoods.The comparison showed that the green roof remained cooler than the white roof, particularly during daylight hours. According to a 2018 project report by University of Hawai'i graduate student Elizabeth Dionne, the white roof had an average daytime surface temperature of 86.7°F (30.4°C), while the green roof averaged 82.6°F (28.1°C).This represented a 4.1°F difference, while over the full 24-hour period the average temperatures were 82°F for the white roof and 80°F for the green roof.The difference became much more striking when peak temperatures were examined. The white roof reached a peak of 113°F, compared with 94.5°F on the green roof, giving a difference of 18.5°F. The report also found that the white roof experienced an average daily temperature fluctuation of 24.9°F, whereas the green roof fluctuated by only 14.1°F. In other words, the planted roof not only reached a lower peak but also experienced less dramatic changes in temperature throughout the day.Several features of the green roof contributed to its cooling effect. Plants release water through evapotranspiration, a process in which water taken up by the roots is released through the leaves. The report explains that evaporation from the leaves has a cooling effect on the surrounding air. The vegetation and growing medium also helped change how heat was absorbed and transferred through the roof.The timing of the daily heat peak provided another indication that the green roof responded differently to sunlight. The white roof reached its highest temperatures between 12:30 and 13:00, while the green roof reached its peak between 14:00 and 15:00. According to the report, this one- to three-hour delay showed that the green roof had “thermal inertia”. Dionne linked this delayed response to the insulating properties of the green roof soil, which could help reduce the amount of heat transferred into a building.The study not only found cooler temperatures on the roof surface. The air immediately above the green roof was also cooler during the daytime. At 2 ft above the roof, the green roof recorded an average daytime temperature of 82.2°F, compared with 85.6°F above the white roof, a difference of 3.4°F. Over 24 hours, the difference at this height was 2.5°F.However, the cooling effect became much less noticeable higher above the roof. At 4 ft, the average daytime temperatures were almost identical: 82.9°F above the green roof and 82.8°F above the white roof. The researchers also found no discernible difference between the roofs at night in the main surface measurements. Overall, the report concluded that green roofs could provide a measurable reduction in daytime surface and nearby air temperatures, while noting that further research using more vegetation and different or deeper growing media would be needed to explore their full potential.
Article Summary: University of Hawaii study found that a planted green roof could stay noticeably cooler than a conventional white roof. The cooling effect was also detected in the air immediately above the roof, where temperatures 2 ft above the green surface averaged 3.4°F lower during the day. The findings suggest that vegetation can help limit rooftop heat and moderate nearby air temperatures.

Article Title: In 2016, Florida’s New Smyrna Beach used living shorelines during Hurricane Matthew; the structures stayed intact despite 90 mph winds

Living shorelines showed less damage after Hurricane Matthew

When Hurricane Matthew struck Florida in October 2016, New Smyrna Beach faced winds of more than 90 miles per hour and water levels around four feet above normal. Along the coast, those conditions put shoreline protection to a serious test. But one demonstration site emerged with an unexpected result. A living shoreline project supported by NOAA and the St Johns River Water Management District remained largely intact after the storm, with minimal erosion. Instead of depending on conventional seawalls or bulkheads, the project used vegetation, sand and limited amounts of rock to stabilise the shoreline while also providing habitat for wildlife. The demonstration area was directly in the path of Matthew's most destructive winds, making its survival particularly notable. Nearby, a building even lost its roof during the storm. Yet the living shoreline structures held firm. The experience offered a striking example of how natural shoreline protection could withstand powerful hurricane conditions.Living shorelines take a different approach from traditional coastal defences.Rather than relying entirely on concrete, bulkheads or seawalls, they incorporate natural materials such as vegetation, sand and limited amounts of rock. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, these materials help shorelines withstand the energy carried by storm surges and waves while also creating habitat for fish and wildlife. The approach is intended to reduce erosion while strengthening the resilience of coastal areas.That distinction became important when Hurricane Matthew arrived. Conventional hardened structures can sometimes increase coastal erosion and provide little habitat. Living shorelines, by contrast, combine coastal protection with ecological benefits. The New Smyrna Beach project therefore served not only as a demonstration of different shoreline techniques, but also as an opportunity to see how those approaches performed when confronted with an actual hurricane.The conditions around New Smyrna Beach were severe enough to expose weaknesses in coastal structures. Winds exceeded 90 miles per hour, a nearby building lost its roof, and water levels rose roughly four feet above normal. The demonstration shoreline also faced north, directly towards the direction from which the most destructive winds arrived. Yet when the storm had passed, NOAA found that the structures were still standing and had suffered minimal erosion.The result was striking because the project was not tested under mild conditions. It faced a major hurricane with strong winds, elevated water and wave energy, making the outcome a useful demonstration of how natural shoreline techniques could perform during a storm. NOAA's assessment was direct: "after the hurricane, all structures in the area were intact, with minimal erosion."Evidence from elsewhere along the coast provided another point of comparison. In the aftermath of Hurricane Matthew, the North Carolina Coastal Federation surveyed shorelines and found no visible damage at the living shorelines it examined. By comparison, at least half of the hardened shorelines in its survey had been damaged, including areas where sediment had been scoured from the front of structures or water had flowed over them, weakening them.The New Smyrna Beach experience therefore became part of a wider picture of how coastal communities might respond to storms. Living shorelines are not simply planted areas beside the water. They are a form of shoreline stabilisation designed to reduce erosion while also supporting habitat and coastal resilience. Hurricane Matthew provided an unusually demanding test, and the New Smyrna Beach demonstration structures emerged from it still standing, with little erosion.
Article Summary: Living shorelines take a different approach from traditional coastal defences. They incorporate natural materials such as vegetation, sand and limited amounts of rock. These materials help shorelines withstand the energy carried by storm surges and waves. The approach is intended to reduce erosion while strengthening the resilience of coastal areas.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.

Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.

The good news is that with a small amount of preparation, done in the right order, you won't lose a single message, photo, or video during the switch.First things first, in order to backup your WhatsApp chats, open the messaging app on your old phone and then head to Settings.
